newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-PRODIGAL SON TO RESTORE THE FAITH.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-PRODIGAL SON TO RESTORE THE FAITH.

text.p: Once or twice in a sporting lifetime a player somehow reflects the mood and characteristics of his nation as surely as any national flag or anthem.

Former Springbok rugby captain Francois Pienaar was a shining example at last year's World Cup, current All Black leader Sean Fitzpatrick remains another. In Welsh rugby, sole responsibility for a million hopes and dreams is suddenly back in the hands of Jonathan Davies.

This weekend, a Cardiff crowd will see something neither they or the 34-year-old Davies ever believed could happen again. The prodigal son will be wearing the red number 10 jersey again and the hymns of thanksgiving have already started in the Arms Park ticket office with the sale of 12,000 extra seats.

Some are saying the return of a fly-half with not many miles left on the clock is no more than short-term expediency for a country gearing up to host the World Cup in 1999, but to focus on box office greed is to miss the point entirely.
For anyone who has followed Welsh rugby's descent from the glory days of the 1970s, Davies's selection is symbolic, poignant and significant all at once.

When he left rugby union in 1988, stung by the criticism which followed a 15-9 home defeat by Romania and seeking security for his family, a large chunk of a country's self- esteem went with him. No-one seriously blamed him for heading north to play rugby league for Widnes, it just left behind a hollow feeling which took a long time to ease.

Davies himself had signalled his departure 18 months earlier, bemoaning the lack of financial support and condescending attitude shown by the Welsh union. "People are just not treated right in rugby union. So when you get the lure of big money, you think 'The hell with it, why not?' If I had to choose between 50 caps or 100,000 pounds ($160,000), I know which I would rather have. Nobody else will look after you."

By the time he went to league, Davies had won 27 caps, helping Wales to the semifinals of the 1987 World Cup and re-establishing the line of great Welsh fly-halves stretching from Cliff Morgan through Barry John to Phil Bennett.

Sharp, enterprising and ever-alert for the try-line, there were nevertheless concerns about how his slender frame would stand up to the demands of rugby league. It took a little time, but between 1989 and 1995 he scored over 2,000 points and won 12 caps for Britain, one of the rare players to represent them in four different postions -- full-back, wing, centre and stand- off.
His final game of league turned out to be for Wales 13 months ago, in another World Cup semifinal against England in Manchester, before he returned to the union game to an inevitable fanfare.

Since then, though, the schoolboy script has taken a darker turn. He did not enjoy the "alien" experience of his first game with Cardiff and his wife Karen was diagnosed with stomach cancer earlier this year. Having lost his father through cancer when he was 14 and with his stepfather also battling the disease, he came close to packing in the game completely.
"This will mean a lot to my family," he said this week. "It might be the turn of luck we need. Karen is good at the moment and I hope she will be proud of me."

Having guided Cardiff to the European Cup semifinals, there must still be an outside chance that Davies could now achieve one of the few honours to elude a man who has captained his country in both codes.
"If I have one last dream it is to play for the British Lions in South Africa. I've never played for the Lions....if I were to be chosen it would round everything off nicely, wouldn't it?"

Australia, whose own 33-year-old fly-half David Knox must now surrender his place as test rugby's oldest number 10, will have other ideas as they seek to complete an unbeaten tour of Europe and some local newspapers are also dubious.
Illustrating two Welsh supporters outside the Arms Park, at least one cartoonist has been quick to puncture the pre-match hype.
"The way Wales have been playing," read the caption, "perhaps Jonathan only wants to be picked every eight years."
